evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2024: annual hours U.S. adults spend on health care time and paperwork
evidence_cards.unit: hours per year per adult (mean over adults with a valid answer), or percent of adults
evidence_cards.definition: Edited annual hours adults report spending on their own visits and prescriptions, on others' visits, on medical bills and insurance, and on health care paperwork; plus the share who cared for a friend or family member in the past 30 days. Reported per week, month or year and converted to hours per year.
evidence_cards.method: Weighted mean (ESAQ person weight ESAQWT24F) with a Taylor-linearised standard error from VARSTR and VARPSU; adults who skipped an item are excluded from that item.
evidence_cards.source_locator: MEPS HC-256 (2024 Full-Year Consolidated): EQMVAM53, EQOVAM53, EQMBAM53, EQPPAM53, EQCARE53, ESAQWT24F
comparability: All U.S. adults who answered the questionnaire, not people with Lyme disease or Long COVID: MEPS cannot identify either condition reliably (AHRQ, 2026-09-24).
Fielded in 2024 only: the questionnaire was funded for that year, so there is no trend and no later update.

Self-reported. MEPS top-coded the annual hours at the 99.5th percentile (Table 13 of the HC-256 documentation: 2,080 hours for own visits, 1,040 for others' visits, 720 for bills, 520 for paperwork), so a few very large values are capped. About 6% of respondents skipped each time item, and MEPS notes that about 20% of those who completed the paper version gave no answer to them.
Hours, not dollars. Converting hours to dollars needs a published wage or value-of-time source shown next to the estimate.

scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire study (title, abstract, methods, and all participant data) is about patients navigating care coordination for long COVID at a post-COVID recovery clinic; Lyme disease is never mentioned anywhere in the text.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a qualitative interview study (n=21) conducted at an Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center post-COVID recovery clinic in August-September 2022, examining how adult patients with long COVID experienced access to care, evaluation, treatment, and ongoing care concerns. Patients described being disbelieved or having symptoms misattributed by providers, confusion about which symptoms to report to which specialist, frustration when tests came back normal or diagnoses were not linked to COVID, and anxiety about long-term effects such as cognitive decline and shortened life expectancy. The authors conclude that healthcare systems are currently unprepared to coordinate care for this new chronic condition, citing a shortage of knowledgeable providers and a lack of evidence-based treatment guidelines. The study reports no dollar costs, no quantified productivity loss, and no formal economic burden estimates; its findings are entirely qualitative/experiential.

contextual_issues: Patients described repeated, fragmented care-seeking across multiple specialists (e.g., cardiology, physical therapy, speech therapy) without the document quantifying number of visits, time, or cost.
Patients reported confusion about which symptoms to report to which specialist, a practical burden of navigating multi-specialty care that is not quantified.

Patients described frustration with normal diagnostic test results or diagnoses not attributed to long COVID, implying repeated/extended diagnostic workups, but no number of tests, visits, or associated cost is given.
Patients reported providers who did not believe or validate their symptoms, described as a barrier to accessing care, but the document does not quantify how this affected time-to-diagnosis or cost.

Patients expressed concern about long-term impacts of long COVID (cognitive decline, Alzheimer's/Parkinson's risk, reduced life expectancy) as a psychological/anticipatory burden, with no quantification offered.

The Limitations section notes many interviewed patients had been experiencing severe symptoms for 1-2 years, suggesting prolonged illness duration in this sample, but this is a descriptive range about the interviewed sample, not a modeled burden estimate with a price year or population-level value.

Authors note a 'critical shortage of providers knowledgeable about this condition' and lack of evidence-based guidelines, implying systemic strain on the care system, but no measured count of provider shortage or guideline gap is given.
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost data (visits, tests, specialist referrals, medications) are reported for this sample.
No direct non-medical cost data (travel, paid help, home modifications) are reported.
No indirect cost data (lost income, productivity loss, caregiving time) are reported, despite participants describing symptoms significantly impacting daily life.

No quantified diagnostic delay (e.g., number of months or visits to reach a long COVID diagnosis) is reported; only a general sample-level descriptive range (1-2 years of severe symptoms) appears in the Limitations section.
No insurance, billing, or coverage/access-barrier data (e.g., denied claims, referral delays tied to insurance) are reported.

Demographic data collected were limited to age and sex only; the document itself states it did not collect broader demographic information, so disparities by race/ethnicity, disability status, veteran status, or socioeconomic status cannot be assessed from this study.

The sample was recruited from a single academic medical center's post-COVID clinic requiring physician referral, so findings may not generalize to patients without access to such specialized care (a limitation the authors themselves note).
comparison_boundaries: This is a single qualitative study of 21 patients recruited from one academic medical center's post-COVID recovery clinic (interviews conducted August-September 2022); its findings cannot be pooled with quantitative cost-of-illness, prevalence, or claims-based estimates from other documents or datasets because it uses a different method (thematic analysis of interview transcripts) and population (clinic-referred, English-speaking adults who self-identified as functioning well before COVID).
No price year, dollar figures, or national-population estimates appear in this document, so none of its findings should be combined numerically with cost or prevalence figures from other sources.

Comparisons the Discussion section draws to other qualitative studies (e.g., UK healthcare workers with long COVID, chronic fatigue syndrome/fibromyalgia patients) are narrative/thematic parallels drawn by the authors, not pooled or re-analyzed data, and should not be treated as a combined dataset.

systemic_gap_caveat.description: The document describes a care-system gap in which primary care providers and specialists lack evidence-based guidelines and training to recognize, evaluate, or treat long COVID, so specialists who find no organic pathology on standard tests and providers who make a diagnosis both remain uncertain how to treat patients, with no coordinated model to manage patients across the many specialists they are referred to.
systemic_gap_caveat.basis: Discussion section statements that 'a critical shortage of providers knowledgeable about this condition is one cause of this unpreparedness,' that 'primary care providers are at a loss due to the lack of evidence-based guidelines on management and treatment of long COVID,' and that specialists 'may conclude that there is no organic pathology' while 'even if a diagnosis is made, providers remain uncertain how to treat patients' (pp. 1298-1299).

decision_relevance.summary: A simulator built from this document could not model dollar costs or prevalence (none are reported), but it could surface the qualitative care-coordination failure points patients experience: provider disbelief, confusing multi-specialist communication, inconclusive or misattributed test results, absence of treatment guidelines, and anxiety about long-term effects. Patients/advocates could use this to articulate and validate the practical burden of navigating care for long COVID. Care delivery teams could use the identified themes (access barriers, evaluation confusion, treatment uncertainty, ongoing care concerns) to redesign referral pathways or consider 'one-stop-shop' multidisciplinary clinic models, which the Discussion explicitly raises as a potential solution. Payers/policy audiences could use the systemic-gap description (provider shortage, lack of guidelines) to motivate investment in long COVID care infrastructure, though this document supplies no cost-effectiveness or budget-impact figures to support a financial business case.
use_cases: Illustrating, for patient/advocate audiences, the specific recurring care-coordination pain points (disbelief, fragmented specialist communication, inconclusive test results, no treatment guidelines) reported by long COVID patients, to support self-advocacy or clinic feedback.

Informing care delivery teams' design of multidisciplinary or 'one-stop-shop' long COVID clinic models and referral/triage communication tools, directly referencing the barriers and facilitators to access described in this qualitative dataset.

Comparisons the Discussion section draws to other qualitative studies (e.g., UK healthcare workers with long COVID, chronic fatigue syndrome/fibromyalgia patients) are narrative/thematic parallels drawn by the authors, not pooled or re-analyzed data, and should not be treated as a combined dataset.

systemic_gap_caveat.description: The document describes a care-system gap in which primary care providers and specialists lack evidence-based guidelines and training to recognize, evaluate, or treat long COVID, so specialists who find no organic pathology on standard tests and providers who make a diagnosis both remain uncertain how to treat patients, with no coordinated model to manage patients across the many specialists they are referred to.
systemic_gap_caveat.basis: Discussion section statements that 'a critical shortage of providers knowledgeable about this condition is one cause of this unpreparedness,' that 'primary care providers are at a loss due to the lack of evidence-based guidelines on management and treatment of long COVID,' and that specialists 'may conclude that there is no organic pathology' while 'even if a diagnosis is made, providers remain uncertain how to treat patients' (pp. 1298-1299).

decision_relevance.summary: A simulator built from this document could not model dollar costs or prevalence (none are reported), but it could surface the qualitative care-coordination failure points patients experience: provider disbelief, confusing multi-specialist communication, inconclusive or misattributed test results, absence of treatment guidelines, and anxiety about long-term effects. Patients/advocates could use this to articulate and validate the practical burden of navigating care for long COVID. Care delivery teams could use the identified themes (access barriers, evaluation confusion, treatment uncertainty, ongoing care concerns) to redesign referral pathways or consider 'one-stop-shop' multidisciplinary clinic models, which the Discussion explicitly raises as a potential solution. Payers/policy audiences could use the systemic-gap description (provider shortage, lack of guidelines) to motivate investment in long COVID care infrastructure, though this document supplies no cost-effectiveness or budget-impact figures to support a financial business case.
use_cases: Illustrating, for patient/advocate audiences, the specific recurring care-coordination pain points (disbelief, fragmented specialist communication, inconclusive test results, no treatment guidelines) reported by long COVID patients, to support self-advocacy or clinic feedback.

Informing care delivery teams' design of multidisciplinary or 'one-stop-shop' long COVID clinic models and referral/triage communication tools, directly referencing the barriers and facilitators to access described in this qualitative dataset.

package.documentation:
## About this simulator

This simulator is built from a qualitative interview study (n=21) conducted August-September 2022 at an Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center post-COVID recovery clinic. The study used thematic analysis of patient interviews to describe experiences accessing care, undergoing evaluation and treatment, and living with ongoing long COVID concerns. It reports **no dollar costs, no income loss figures, no prevalence estimates, and no national or population-level data**. Because of this, every output here is an illustrative count (specialists, testing rounds, and barrier themes) built by the analysis to represent the study's recurring qualitative themes, not a measured average reported by the study itself. Only the severe-symptom-duration input (1-2 years) is a range the document itself states, drawn from its Limitations section.

## Limitation: systemic care-system gap

The document describes a limitation in the care system itself, not just in its own data: it attributes patients' coordination difficulties to a shortage of providers knowledgeable about long COVID and to the absence of evidence-based management and treatment guidelines, so that even specialists who find no organic pathology on standard tests, and providers who do make a diagnosis, remain uncertain how to treat patients, with no coordinated pathway across the many specialists patients are referred to (Discussion section, pp. 1298-1299). This is a limitation of the evidence and care-delivery system producing long COVID guidance, distinct from any limitation in how this particular estimate was measured.

## Scope notes

The sample was recruited from a single academic medical center's post-COVID clinic requiring physician referral, so findings may not generalize to patients without access to such specialized care. Demographic data collected were limited to age and sex, and the document does not report a sex- or gender-based difference in findings. No claims-based, subgroup-disaggregation, or research-funding-gap limitation applies to this document, as it contains no claims data, no pooled quantitative value, and no funding comparison. Because this document is purely qualitative, its findings should not be numerically combined with cost-of-illness, prevalence, or claims-based estimates from other sources.
